sources.title: ADA: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes—2026
ADA: Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises—2026
Endocrine Society: Glucocorticoid-Induced Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult has an A1C in the diabetes range on routine screening but no unequivocal hyperglycemic symptoms. What is the correct diagnostic principle?
choices: Confirm the abnormal result with an appropriate repeat or second diagnostic test unless unequivocal hyperglycemia is present
Diagnose diabetes from any single abnormal home glucose value
Exclude diabetes because symptoms are required
Use continuous glucose monitoring as the sole validated diagnostic test
rationales: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires confirmatory abnormal testing.
Home readings can guide assessment but do not replace standardized diagnostic confirmation.
Type 2 diabetes can be asymptomatic.
Current ADA guidance does not recommend CGM as the sole screening or diagnostic method.
questions.explanation: Confirmation reduces misclassification from biologic variation, laboratory error, or factors that make one test unreliable.

questions.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes has abdominal pain, vomiting, glucose 420 mg/dL, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate. Which hormonal shift drives this crisis?
choices: Insulin deficiency with excess counterregulatory hormones promotes lipolysis, ketogenesis, and hyperglycemia
Excess insulin blocks glucose uptake and causes ketogenesis
Isolated aldosterone deficiency directly creates ketone bodies
High thyroid hormone suppresses hepatic glucose production
rationales: Low effective insulin and high glucagon/catecholamine/cortisol signaling increase hepatic glucose output and free-fatty-acid conversion to ketones.
Excess insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis.
Aldosterone affects sodium and potassium balance but is not the primary ketone-generating defect.
Thyroid hormone does not explain the insulin-deficient ketoacid pattern.
questions.explanation: DKA is both a hyperglycemic and ketoacidotic state, so treatment must address volume, insulin deficiency, potassium shifts, and the precipitating cause.

questions.question: An older adult with type 2 diabetes presents with profound dehydration, confusion, glucose 980 mg/dL, high effective osmolality, minimal ketones, and near-normal pH. Which diagnosis is most likely?
choices: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Diabetic ketoacidosis as the only possible hyperglycemic crisis
Primary adrenal crisis
Insulinoma
rationales: Extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, dehydration, and minimal ketoacidosis are characteristic of HHS.
DKA has substantial ketonemia and metabolic acidosis, though overlap syndromes can occur.
Adrenal crisis tends toward hypoglycemia or normal glucose with hypotension and electrolyte abnormalities.
Insulinoma causes hypoglycemia rather than severe hyperglycemia.
questions.explanation: Residual insulin may suppress major ketogenesis while remaining insufficient to prevent severe hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis.

questions.question: A lean adolescent has polyuria, weight loss, hyperglycemia, positive islet autoantibodies, and low C-peptide. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction has reduced endogenous insulin production
Peripheral insulin resistance has increased endogenous insulin secretion
Excess glucagon has increased C-peptide production
Exogenous insulin use raises C-peptide concentration
rationales: Islet autoantibodies and low C-peptide support autoimmune loss of endogenous beta-cell insulin secretion.
Early insulin resistance often has preserved or elevated endogenous insulin and C-peptide.
C-peptide is released with endogenous insulin, not glucagon.
Injected insulin contains no C-peptide and does not directly raise it.
questions.explanation: C-peptide distinguishes endogenous insulin secretion from exogenous insulin and helps classify atypical presentations in context.

questions.question: A patient has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, diffuse goiter, elevated free T4, and suppressed TSH. Which level of dysfunction is most likely?
choices: Primary thyroid hormone excess suppressing pituitary TSH through negative feedback
Primary pituitary failure causing thyroid overproduction
Primary hypothyroidism with compensatory TSH suppression
Isolated adrenal insufficiency increasing thyroid hormone binding
rationales: High circulating thyroid hormone suppresses TSH when the thyroid gland is the source of excess hormone.
Pituitary failure would tend to lower thyroid hormone rather than raise it.
Primary hypothyroidism generally raises TSH when the pituitary is intact.
Adrenal insufficiency does not produce this classic biochemical pattern.
questions.explanation: Interpreting paired pituitary and target-gland hormones localizes endocrine dysfunction more reliably than symptoms alone.

questions.question: A patient with headaches and visual-field loss has low free T4 with a TSH value in the laboratory reference range. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
choices: The TSH is inappropriately normal for the low free T4, raising concern for central hypothyroidism
A normal TSH always excludes hypothyroidism
The thyroid gland is clearly producing excess hormone
The pattern confirms primary hyperparathyroidism
rationales: When free T4 is low, an intact pituitary should raise TSH; a normal value can therefore be pathologically inappropriate.
TSH alone can miss central hypothyroidism.
Free T4 is low, not high.
Parathyroid disease is evaluated through calcium/PTH physiology, not this pattern.
questions.explanation: Endocrine values must be judged against the expected feedback response, not only the printed reference interval.

questions.question: A patient has fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, orthostatic hypotension, sodium 128 mEq/L, and potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Which defect best unifies the findings?
choices: Primary adrenal cortex failure causing cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with elevated ACTH
Secondary adrenal suppression causing excess aldosterone
Primary hyperaldosteronism
Pheochromocytoma with chronic mineralocorticoid excess
rationales: Primary adrenal failure lowers cortisol and aldosterone; elevated ACTH can cause hyperpigmentation, while mineralocorticoid loss causes hyperkalemia and volume depletion.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency usually preserves aldosterone through RAAS and does not typically cause hyperkalemia or ACTH-driven pigmentation.
Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and often hypokalemia.
Pheochromocytoma causes catecholamine excess, not this electrolyte pattern.
questions.explanation: Pigmentation and potassium status help distinguish primary adrenal failure from central suppression.

questions.question: A patient abruptly stops long-term high-dose prednisone and develops profound weakness, nausea, and hypotension during an infection. What is the primary concern?
choices: Glucocorticoid-induced hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression with inadequate cortisol response to stress
Immediate primary hyperaldosteronism
Permanent thyroid-stimulating hormone excess
Insulinoma caused by glucocorticoid withdrawal
rationales: Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress CRH and ACTH; abrupt withdrawal can leave inadequate endogenous cortisol, especially during physiologic stress.
Glucocorticoid withdrawal does not cause primary aldosterone excess.
The syndrome is not explained by TSH excess.
Insulinoma is unrelated to chronic glucocorticoid suppression.
questions.explanation: Potential adrenal crisis is time sensitive. Prevention includes appropriate tapering and stress-dose planning when indicated.

questions.question: A patient has resistant hypertension, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin, and elevated aldosterone. Which diagnosis is most likely?
choices: Primary aldosteronism
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Central diabetes insipidus
rationales: Autonomous aldosterone promotes sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen loss, hypertension, and suppression of renin.
Adrenal insufficiency produces low aldosterone, hypotension, and often hyperkalemia.
SIADH causes water retention and hyponatremia without this aldosterone-renin pattern.
Diabetes insipidus causes dilute polyuria and possible hypernatremia.
questions.explanation: The renin-aldosterone relationship distinguishes autonomous secretion from secondary RAAS activation.

questions.question: A patient has episodic pounding headache, diaphoresis, palpitations, and severe paroxysmal hypertension; biochemical testing supports catecholamine-secreting tumor. Why must preoperative pharmacologic sequencing be carefully planned?
choices: Alpha-adrenergic blockade is established before beta blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Beta blockade alone should always precede any alpha blockade
Both alpha and beta receptors must remain fully stimulated before surgery
Diuretics alone eliminate catecholamine release
rationales: Blocking beta receptors first can leave alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and precipitate dangerous hypertension; expert-guided alpha blockade precedes beta blockade when needed.
Beta-first sequencing can be hazardous.
Continued unopposed catecholamine stimulation increases perioperative risk.
Diuretics do not stop tumor catecholamine secretion and may worsen volume depletion.
questions.explanation: Mechanism determines treatment order. Suspected pheochromocytoma requires specialist coordination rather than routine outpatient antihypertensive escalation.
